c.tagline: The Garden City and beating heart of the Ashanti kingdom, ringed by kente and gold.

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'dropping' taxis are unmetered — agree the price before setting off. App rides (Uber, Bolt, Yango) are widely available, usually cheaper than street taxis and avoid haggling.

emergency.note: 112 works as a general emergency line from mobile phones; 192 reaches the fire service. Response can be slow, so many visitors go directly to a private hospital.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets in the dense crowds of Kejetia Market and Adum, especially with phones out.

hood_desc: The dense central business district and main shopping core, packed with stores, banks, forex bureaux and street stalls; the convenient, if hectic, walkable heart of the city for first-timers.

An upscale, leafy residential area south-west of the centre with many of Kumasi's better hotels, restaurants and bars; suits travellers wanting comfortable dining and nightlife within reach of the centre.
A quieter, more spacious residential and commercial district in the south with a shopping mall, offices and mid-range hotels; good for a calmer base with modern conveniences.

A leafy, affluent suburb about 4 km south of Adum, strung along Melcom Road and the Ahodwo Roundabout, with the biggest concentration of independent hotels and restaurants outside the centre. It suits travellers who want space and quiet and do not mind a short taxi ride into town.

water.note: Drink bottled or sealed sachet water; avoid tap.

transit.hours: Tro-tros and shared taxis run from early morning until mid-evening; after dark, app rides and taxis fill the gap.
transit.note: Kumasi has no metro or tram and no regular passenger rail. The city moves by tro-tro (shared minibus), shared and 'dropping' taxis, and ride-hailing apps.
transit.pay: Tro-tro and taxi fares are paid in cash (Ghanaian Cedi) to the driver or mate; there is no transit card. Mobile-money is common for app rides and many shops.

bus: Intercity coaches to Accra and beyond (STC, VIP, VVIP, OA Travel & Tours)
train: No regular passenger rail service (the Kumasi-Accra line is not in scheduled operation)

transit.m: Airport taxi to Adum / city centre (~20 min)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving small change for good service is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Fufu with light soup
food.desc: Pounded cassava and plantain worked into a smooth elastic mound, dropped into a peppery tomato and ginger broth with goat, chicken or fish.

places.name: Yaa Serwaa Chop Bar
places.note: Traditional chop bar serving pounded fufu and soups the Ashanti way, generous and inexpensive.

places.name: Plus 2 Pub
places.note: Often called the best fufu joint in Kumasi, with a wide choice of soups and proteins.

places.name: Kejetia Market food stalls
places.note: Where market traders eat; about the cheapest and most authentic bowl in the city.

food.name: Waakye
food.desc: Rice and beans cooked with sorghum leaves until reddish-brown, piled with shito, gari, spaghetti, boiled egg and fried plantain from a roadside pan.

places.name: Plus 2 Pub
places.note: Serves waakye alongside jollof and banku, useful if your group wants different things.

places.name: Oseikrom Restaurant
places.note: Local favourite for big portions of Ghanaian staples at everyday prices.

places.name: Morning waakye sellers around Adum
places.note: Street vendors set up from dawn near the shops; ask for it wrapped in leaves.

food.name: Banku with grilled tilapia
food.desc: Sour fermented corn and cassava dough eaten by hand with charcoal-grilled tilapia, hot pepper and onion relish, and a bowl of okro stew.

places.name: Plus 2 Pub
places.note: Banku with tilapia or herrings is a house standard, and the grill runs into the evening.

places.name: Oseikrom Restaurant
places.note: Reliable for banku, fufu and stews without the tourist mark-up.

places.name: Grill spots along the Ahodwo roundabout
places.note: Cluster of open-air tilapia grills that fill up after dark, best from around 7pm.

food.name: Nkate nkwan with omo tuo
food.desc: Rich groundnut soup thickened with peanut paste and chilli, served with rice balls; the Ashanti Sunday dish and a Kumasi household benchmark.

places.name: Abenaas Kitchen
places.note: Homestyle cooking praised for its groundnut soup and rotating menu of traditional dishes.

places.name: Yaa Serwaa Chop Bar
places.note: Chop-bar version cooked in large pots, at its best around midday.

places.name: Kejetia Market food stalls
places.note: Market cooks serve it with rice balls or fufu for a couple of cedis.

food.name: Kontomire stew with ampesi
food.desc: Cocoyam leaves stewed with palm oil, egusi seeds and smoked fish, eaten with boiled yam, plantain and cocoyam; deeply Ashanti home cooking.

places.name: Abenaas Kitchen
places.note: Homestyle kitchen where the daily menu rotates through the classic village stews.

places.name: Yaa Serwaa Chop Bar
places.note: Chop bars are the right place for kontomire; ask what has been cooked that morning.

places.name: Kejetia Market food stalls
places.note: Served with boiled yam and plantain to traders throughout the working day.

food.name: Kelewele
food.desc: Ripe plantain cubes tossed in ginger, chilli, nutmeg and cloves and deep-fried until caramelised, sold in paper cones with roasted peanuts.

places.name: Evening kelewele stands in Adum
places.note: Women fry it fresh on the street from late afternoon; the smell finds you first.

places.name: Kejetia Market food stalls
places.note: Cheap cones sold all day among the market aisles, often with groundnuts.

places.name: Plus 2 Pub
places.note: Sit-down option if you want it as a side rather than eating standing up.

food.name: Sobolo
food.desc: Deep-red hibiscus infusion steeped with ginger, cloves and pineapple skin, served very cold and lightly sweet; Ghana's default soft drink.

places.name: Kejetia Market drink sellers
places.note: Sold in chilled bottles from coolers throughout the market, the cheapest in town.

places.name: Abenaas Kitchen
places.note: Homemade version served with meals rather than a bottled commercial one.

places.name: Street vendors around Adum
places.note: Easy to find near the shops and lorry park, usually spiced with plenty of ginger.

food.name: Palm wine (nsafufuo)
food.desc: Sap tapped from palm trees and drunk the same day, cloudy and faintly sweet in the morning, sharper and stronger by evening as it ferments.

places.name: Palm wine spots on the Kumasi outskirts
places.note: Roadside drinking spots on the edge of town get fresh tapping deliveries each morning.

places.name: Kejetia Market drink sellers
places.note: Sold from jerrycans by the calabash; buy early in the day for the sweeter version.

places.name: Yaa Serwaa Chop Bar
places.note: Chop bars often keep palm wine alongside the food, the traditional pairing with fufu.

landmarks: Manhyia Palace Museum
The seat of the Asante king, where a museum inside the 1925 palace chronicles the powerful kingdom's history, regalia and living royal traditions.
Kejetia Market (Kumasi Central Market)
One of West Africa's largest markets, a labyrinth of thousands of stalls selling kente cloth, beads, spices and everything else imaginable.
Okomfo Anokye Sword Site
A legendary sword planted in the ground three centuries ago by the priest who founded the Asante union; tradition says it can never be removed.
Prempeh II Jubilee Museum
An intimate museum at the Kumasi Cultural Centre displaying royal artifacts, including a replica of the sacred Golden Stool at the heart of Asante identity.
Kumasi Fort and Ghana Armed Forces Museum
A British-built 1820 fort that withstood an Asante siege, now a military museum recounting colonial battles and Ghana's wartime service.
St. Peter's Cathedral Basilica
Kumasi's stately Catholic basilica, a century-old landmark of twin towers and stained glass that anchors the city's Christian heritage.
Rattray Park
A modern leisure park with dancing fountains, gardens and jogging paths, offering Kumasi families a polished green retreat named for a colonial-era anthropologist.
KNUST Botanical Gardens
A shady university arboretum of towering tropical trees and butterflies, a peaceful study in Ghana's plant life on the KNUST campus.
Kumasi Zoo
A 1957 wildlife sanctuary between the Kejetia terminal and the old racecourse, home to around 40 native Ghanaian species and thousands of roosting bats in its trees.
Centre for National Culture
A 1956 crafts and cultural complex in central Kumasi with kente-weaving workshops and exhibition halls celebrating Ashanti heritage.

train.note: No usable passenger train serves Kumasi. Ghana's revived services run in the Western Region on the short Kojokrom-Sekondi-Takoradi line, and the new standard-gauge Tema-Mpakadan line near Accra was commissioned but not carrying scheduled passengers as of mid-2026. There is no online rail booking - use coaches instead.

intl.to: Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso) - via the Paga border
intl.op: STC / regional operators — tickets at the Kumasi STC terminal
STC — tickets at the Kumasi STC terminal

bus.note: STC (Intercity STC Coaches) is the state operator and the most reliable, running from its Kumasi terminal to Accra in about 5 hours and on the international routes to Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire, both of which take a day or more. VIP and OA Travel also run the Accra route frequently. Carry your passport and yellow fever certificate for the border crossings; buy tickets at the terminal.

ferry.note: Kumasi is inland in the Ashanti region with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. Ghana's lake ferry runs on Lake Volta between Akosombo and Yeji, several hours to the east.

half.name: Bonwire Kente Village
half.blurb: The celebrated birthplace of kente weaving, where clacking looms produce Ghana's iconic royal cloth and weavers happily demonstrate their intricate craft.

half.name: Lake Bosomtwe
half.blurb: A sacred meteorite-crater lake ringed by forested hills south of Kumasi, where Asante fishermen still paddle traditional wooden planks across holy waters.
